questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Definite Integral of a Vector-Valued Function
questions.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each componentt separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}⟨2{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{0}^{1}2{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨(2{e}^{t}){|}_{0}^{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{1}⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{1}-2{e}^{0},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡1-\operatorname{sin}⁡0⟩ \\  & =⟨2e-2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t+1},\,12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)⟩\text{d}t=⟨\int {e}^{t+1}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)={e}^{t+1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t+1}\text{d}t={e}^{t+1}+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=3t.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 12\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{12}{3}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =4(-\operatorname{cos}⁡u)+{c}_{2} \\  & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t+1},\,12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{e}^{t+1}+{c}_{1},\,-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t+1},\,-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t+1},\,-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{4}),\,{e}^{t-1}⟩\text{d}t=⟨\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{4})\,\text{d}t,\,\int {e}^{t-1}\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{4}),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=\frac{t}{4}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}t=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot 4\text{d}u \\  & =8\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =8(-\operatorname{cos}⁡u)+{c}_{1} \\  & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{4})+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)={e}^{t-1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t-1}\text{d}t={e}^{t-1}+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{4}),\,{e}^{t-1}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{4})+{c}_{1},\,{e}^{t-1}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{4}),\,{e}^{t-1}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{4}),\,{e}^{t-1}⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the following integral of a vector-valued function. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}⟨\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{2+\operatorname{sec}⁡t},\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨$
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $⟩$
questions.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}⟨\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{2+\operatorname{sec}⁡t},\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{2+\operatorname{sec}⁡t}\,\text{d}t,\,{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

For the first component, let $u=2+\operatorname{sec}⁡t$, so $\text{d}u=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{2+\operatorname{sec}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+\operatorname{sec}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second component, we integrate directly:

$$
\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}⟨\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t}{2+\operatorname{sec}⁡t},\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+\operatorname{sec}⁡t){|}_{0}^{\pi /3},\,-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{0}^{\pi /3}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3),\,-4\,(\frac{1}{2}-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨ln\,(\frac{4}{3}),\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨ln\,(\frac{4}{3}),\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨2{e}^{-t}\,,6{t}^{2}-2⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨2{e}^{-t}\,,6{t}^{2}-2⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 2{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t,\int 6{t}^{2}-2\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{e}^{-t}+{c}_{1},\,2{t}^{3}-2t+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(0)=⟨1,\,-4⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0)=⟨-2{e}^{0}+{c}_{1},\,2(0)^{3}-2(0)+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,-4⟩ \\ ⟨-2+{c}_{1},\,0+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=3$ and ${c}_{2}=-4.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨-2{e}^{-t}+3,\,2{t}^{3}-2t-4⟩.
$$
